items.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Yeah. Winard Harper was saying the same thing.

ctx.x: It’s relative. I would say it’s — these days it probably is hard to be a jazz musician because you have situations where you have so many musicians and so relatively few places to play, and particularly places that pay anything decent. I mean there was a time I hear about or read about, or I’ve read about and have been told about, because I’ve done a bunch of interviews myself for the National Jazz Museum of Harlem, their “Harlem Speaks” series, I co-produced that and did dozens of interviews. And you hear these…

Yeah. Winard Harper was saying the same thing. And it’s rather ironic that in one sense jazz has become much more popular and healthy in academia, but that curve going up is sort of matched by the curve going down.

Right, right. So I think the key would be to make sure that those students are prepared. Say listen, it’s great to be an instrumentalist and to know how to do that and to be as good as you can with that, but that in the current marketplace you need to definitely be well- rounded, which a liberal arts education is supposed to give you, and to have some specific skill sets that you can apply in other areas other than music, but even in music there are any number of things that are needed. Certainly fundamentally…
